newsitem.title: GERMANY: German debt and futures suffer in late dealings.
newsitem.headline: German debt and futures suffer in late dealings.

text.p: German Bunds and futures suffered from losses in late dealings on Thursday as the failure of September Bund futures to break a key level and worries about the German yield curve prompted selling.
At 1525 GMT, DTB September Bund futures were down 30 basis points at 103.06 as the contract again failed to stay above 103.50 during a session of relatively active dealings.

"There's not enough support in the market for us to stay above 103.50 right now," said one dealer, noting that the contract has failed on several occassions in the last two weeks to stay above the level seen as necessary for more gains.
Dealers looked for September futures to trade from 102.90 to 103.20 on Friday ahead of U.S. July jobs data at 1230 GMT.

German debt prices slipped but then recovered in line with U.S. Treasury prices after U.S. second quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data showed growth at 2.2 percent compared with 5.9 percent in the first quarter. The second quarter data was above market expectations for growth of 1.9 percent.

But domestic factors also played a key role in the German debt market as worries about the flattening of the yield curve, due to worries about how the Bundesbank will react to the weak mark, was causing investors to sell and buy U.S. debt.

"We saw a lot of Far East investors today getting out of positions in five-year debt," said one dealer. "The flattening yield curve is sending money to the U.S. because people are not sure how the Bundesbank will react."

Dealers explained that domestic investors appeared to have been the most rattled by suggestions the Bundesbank might feel obliged to raise interest rates in order to boost the mark and stem the inflow of imported inflation.
At the moment economists say the softer mark is helping pave the way for higher import prices which will eventually filter through to the cost of living index.
